Idol
ī-d'l
n. (rendering Hebrew 'elīl, pesel, gillūl, and Greek eidōlon)
From Greek eidōlon, an image, phantom, or appearance, from eidos, form — the root idea is a look, a mere appearance. That is already a judgment: an idol is a seeming. The Hebrew words are blunter still. 'elīl is a diminutive playing on 'ēl, God — a godlet, a nothing; pesel is a carved thing; and gillūl, Ezekiel's favourite term, is related to a word for dung.

Biblical Definition

An idol is anything given the worship due to God alone, and Scripture attacks it on two fronts at once. First, idols are nothing: “we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is none other God but one” (1Co 8:4). They have no being, no power, and no claim. “Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands” (Psa 115:4), and the psalm proceeds with devastating simplicity — mouths that speak not, eyes that see not, ears that hear not — concluding that they that make them are like unto them, which is the deepest thing Scripture says about idolatry: the worshipper is conformed to what he worships. Habakkuk presses the absurdity of the manufacture: “What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it…that the maker of his work trusteth therein, to make dumb idols?” (Hab 2:18). Second, and without contradiction, the worship of idols is real traffic with demons — the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils, and not to God. So the idol is nothing and the idolatry is deadly. The second commandment therefore forbids not merely other gods but images of the true God: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above” (Exo 20:4). And the New Testament shews the gospel's effect in one clause — ye turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God — conversion described as a change of masters.

Webster 1828 Definition

An image or anything else given the worship due to God alone; in Scripture nothing in itself, the work of men's hands, yet the occasion of real traffic with devils, forbidden by the second commandment even as a likeness of the true God, and abandoned at conversion.

IDOL, n. 1. An image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship; a pagan deity.

2. An image or representation of any kind, used in worship; and hence, in Scripture, forbidden even when intended as a representation of the true God. Exod. 20.

3. A person or thing loved and honored to adoration; that on which the heart is set. Covetousness, which is idolatry. Col. 3.

4. Anything on which we set our affections; that to which we indulge an excessive and sinful attachment.

5. The Greek eidolon is a form or appearance merely; the Hebrew elil signifies a thing of nought, and gillulim a term of contempt. The names themselves pronounce the judgment.

Key Scripture

Exodus 20:4 — "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:"

Psalm 115:4 — "Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands."

1 Corinthians 8:4 — "As concerning therefore the eating of those things that are offered in sacrifice unto idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is none other God but one."

1 Thessalonians 1:9 — "For they themselves shew of us what manner of entering in we had unto you, and how ye turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God;"

Modern Corruption

Idolatry is treated as an extinct problem of carved images, so that the second commandment is thought to have no modern application — while Scripture names covetousness as idolatry and the making of images of God remains as forbidden as it ever was.

expand to see more

The second commandment forbids two distinct things, and the second is regularly forgotten. It forbids other gods, and it forbids images — including images of the true God. Israel's golden calf was not offered to a rival deity; Aaron proclaimed a feast to the LORD, and the sin was worshipping the true God by a likeness of His own devising. Deuteronomy gives the reason explicitly: ye saw no manner of similitude on the day the LORD spake unto you in Horeb. This is why the Reformed churches removed images and why the regulative principle of worship follows from the commandment rather than being an addition to it. The question in worship is never what seems helpful but what God has commanded, and He has not commanded that He be represented.

The other half of the neglect is the assumption that idolatry ended with paganism. Paul twice defines covetousness as idolatry, and Job disclaims making gold his hope. An idol is whatever the heart trusts, fears, and serves in God's place, and it need not be carved to be worshipped — money, reputation, security, family, and the self all take the office readily. The Psalm's conclusion is the warning that gives the doctrine its bite: they that make them are like unto them. Men become like what they worship, growing as deaf and blind as their idols; and by the same law, beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, we are changed into the same image, from glory to glory. The remedy is not merely to demolish the idol but to turn, as the Thessalonians did, to the living and true God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew names idols with contempt: 'elīl, a godlet or nothing; pesel, a carved image; gillūl, a term Ezekiel uses connected with dung; massēkâh, a molten image. Greek eidōlon is a mere appearance, and eidōlolatria is idol-service.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'elīl (H457) — a thing of nought, a godlet; a contemptuous diminutive echoing 'ēl, God. Used in Psa 96:5, all the gods of the nations are idols.

Hebrew pesel (H6459) — a graven image, something hewn; the word in the second commandment (Exo 20:4).

Hebrew gillūl (H1544) — idols; Ezekiel's characteristic term, some 39 times in that book, connected with a root for dung-pellets.

Greek eidōlon (G1497) — an image, a phantom, an idol; from eidos, form or appearance — the name itself denies the thing substance.

Greek eidōlolatria (G1495) — idolatry, idol-service; listed among the works of the flesh (Gal 5:20) and identified with covetousness (Col 3:5).

Usage

"Of the prohibition: thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image (Exo 20:4); ye saw no manner of similitude (Deu 4:15)."

"Of the emptiness of idols: their idols are silver and gold (Psa 115:4); an idol is nothing in the world (1Co 8:4); what profiteth the graven image? (Hab 2:18)."

"Of the heart's idols and of conversion: covetousness, which is idolatry (Col 3:5); ye turned to God from idols (1Th 1:9); little children, keep yourselves from idols (1Jo 5:21)."
